name: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070
memory_bandwidth_basis: GDDR7 28 Gbps data rate x 192-bit / 8 = 672 GB/s. Both numbers are printed directly by the RTX Blackwell architecture whitepaper, Table 6 (GeForce RTX 5070 vs 4070 vs 3070): 'Memory Clock (Data Rate) 28 Gbps', 'Memory Bandwidth 672 GB/sec', 'Memory Interface 192-bit'. AUDIT CORRECTION 2026-10-04: the basis previously read 'GDDR7 24 Gbps data rate x 192-bit / 8 = 672 GB/s', which is arithmetically false - 24 Gbps x 192-bit / 8 = 576 GB/s, not 672. The stored 672 GB/s was always right; only the stated derivation was wrong. 28 Gbps is confirmed independently by NVIDIA's GeForce RTX 5070 Family product page spec table.

notes: Entry-level Blackwell consumer part. 12 GB GDDR7 on a 192-bit bus at 28 Gbps, 672 GB/s. 250 W TGP. AUDIT 2026-10-04: ALL SEVEN flops rows in this record were wrong, and the memory bandwidth basis was wrong, and the error pattern is diagnostic. Every stored figure had been derived by doubling the record's own (also wrong) fp32 value of 29.4 rather than read off the whitepaper table: fp16 = 2 x 29.4 = 58.7, fp8 = 4 x 29.4 = 117.4, fp4 = 8 x 29.4 = 234.8. The whitepaper's actual figures are fp32 30.9, fp16 61.7, fp8 123.5, fp4 493.9 - i.e. FP4 is 4x FP8, not 2x, so the record had FP4 understated by 2.1x on top of the shared ~5% base error. The fp32 value 29.4 matches no published clock for this part: the whitepaper Table 6 gives 'GPU Boost Clock (MHz) 2512' (= 6144 cores x 2 x 2512 MHz = 30.87 TFLOPS -> 30.9) and NVIDIA's product page gives boost 2.51 GHz / base 2.33 GHz. OLD VALUES, all corrected: fp32 29.4 -> 30.9; fp16 58.7 -> 61.7; bf16 58.7 -> 61.7; fp8 dense 117.4 -> 123.5; fp8 sparse 234.8 -> 246.9; fp4 dense 234.8 -> 493.9; fp4 sparse 469.6 -> 987.8; memory_bandwidth_basis '24 Gbps' -> '28 Gbps'. Internal cross-check that the correction is right: the sibling record nvidia-rtx-5070-ti stores fp32 43.9 and 896 GB/s, both of which reproduce exactly from its own whitepaper row (8960 x 2 x 2452 MHz; 28 Gbps x 256-bit / 8), so this record was the odd one out within its own family. Dense/sparse FLAGS were correct on every row and did not need changing - the failure here was arithmetic, not the inverted-flag class. The 12GB VRAM remains the critical constraint for local LLM inference: a 70B model at 4-bit quantization needs ~35GB, which exceeds this card's capacity. Suitable for models up to ~13B at 4-bit or ~7B at 8-bit. Lowest-VRAM part in the 50-series and the first to be genuinely capacity- rather than compute-constrained for LLM workloads.
